title: Volume 8 · Customise Without Code: Property Setters, Custom Fields and Custom DocTypes
subtitle: Lessons 1–10: what a functional consultant may change in the browser, what survives an upgrade, and how to say no to code
outcomes: Draw the line between configuration in the browser and customisation that needs a developer
Rename, hide, reorder and enforce fields with property setters that survive an upgrade
Add custom fields and a custom DocType with a child table without touching a file
Prove a customisation survives a migration, and keep a change register a successor can read

slides.title: Configuration ends where a file begins
bullets: Everything in Customize Form, a property setter, a custom field or the DocType editor is configuration and belongs to you
Anything that needs a file in an app, a hook or a script is development and belongs to somebody else
The line is not about difficulty, it is about who can reverse the change without a deployment
Say the line out loud in the first workshop, so a requirement does not drift into code by accident
Every configuration change is recorded in a register, because it is invisible until it breaks something

rows: Undo in the browser, not a deploy

slides.notes: The most expensive sentence in a project is 'it's only a small change'. Small changes that need a file still need a deployment, a test and a rollback, and nobody budgeted for that. Draw the line in the first workshop, in writing, while everyone is still friendly.

slides.title: Change the form without changing the DocType
bullets: A property setter records an override on top of the standard definition, so the standard stays intact underneath
Rename a label, make a field mandatory or read-only, hide it, or move it within its section
Setters survive a migration, which is why they are the consultant's tool and hand-edited DocTypes are not
Keep the list short and justified, because twenty setters is a design problem wearing a configuration hat
Every setter goes in the register with the reason the client asked for it

rows: Open Customize Form for the DocType
Form editor with the standard layout
Rename a label the client dislikes
Hide a field the business never uses
Record each change in the register

slides.notes: Property setters are the highest-leverage tool a functional consultant has, and the most abused. Each one is a small divergence from standard behaviour that the next consultant has to discover. Keep them few, documented, and named after the client's own language.

slides.title: Add what the business needs and nothing else
bullets: A custom field is a real column with a real type, so choose the type carefully the first time
Place it deliberately: after which field, in which section, and whether it shows in the list view
A field nobody filters or reports on is a field nobody needed
Defaults and options are configuration; conditional mandatory rules generally are not
Name fields for the business, not the database, because the label is what the client reads

rows: Create a custom field on Sales Invoice
New field in the form editor
Place it after the customer address
Show it in the list view
Save, then open an existing invoice
Field present on old records too
Add a report column using it

slides.notes: The test for a custom field is not whether the client asked for it, but whether anyone filters, prints or reports on it. If the answer is no, it becomes an empty box that someone will eventually fill with the wrong thing. Ask the reporting question before you create the column.

slides.title: One field, three audiences
bullets: The field must be visible where the work happens, which is usually the form and the list, not a report nobody opens
It must be hidden or read-only where it would mislead, which means checking it under a second role
It must survive a migration: refresh the form and confirm the field is still placed correctly
Old records must still open, because a custom field added today appears on documents from last year
If the field feeds a report, check the report returns rows before you call it done

rows: Log in as a normal user

slides.notes: Customisation without verification is decoration. The second-role check catches the commonest failure, which is a field that a sales user can edit when finance assumed it was locked down.

slides.title: A new document you build in the browser
bullets: The DocType editor creates a real table, so the naming and the fields are decisions with consequences
Choose the naming series before the first record exists, because changing it later breaks links
Submittable suits anything with a lifecycle and a freeze; keep it simple unless the lifecycle is real
Permissions come next, or the new document is visible to everyone or nobody
A custom DocType is a commitment: it becomes something the client supports after you leave

rows: Create a DocType from the DocType list
Create one record to prove it

slides.notes: The naming decision is the one people regret. A DocType created with a hash or a plain number cannot be renumbered once records exist, and every link to it depends on those names. Decide the series before the first save, and write the decision in the register.

slides.title: Lines inside a document you built
bullets: A child table turns one survey into many findings without creating a document per finding
The child DocType carries the fields; the parent decides how many rows and what order
Grid columns and their widths are a usability decision, not decoration
Anything the client will sum, count or report per row belongs in the table, not in a long text field
Child tables are edited in the browser like any other, and they survive migrations the same way

rows: Create a child DocType for findings
Add a table field on the parent DocType
Set the child DocType on that field
Set column widths and in-list visibility

slides.notes: The distinction between a child table and a text field decides whether the client can ever report on the data. If the answer to a question needs a count of findings by severity, it has to be rows. Ask the reporting question again, at design time.

slides.title: Sections, columns and the three-second form
bullets: A form that a new user can complete in three seconds is the goal, and layout is most of it
Group related fields into sections and name the section the way the business talks
Two columns is usually right; three becomes a scanning problem on a laptop screen
Move the fields the client types first to the top, because order is a form of training
Test the layout with a real user on a real screen before calling it finished

rows: Split the form into business sections
Move the typed-first fields to the top
First tab stops in the right order
Ask a real user to complete it

slides.notes: Layout work looks cosmetic and is not: it is the difference between a form people use correctly and a form they fill with guesses. Time a real user on a real task, and treat any hesitation as a design defect rather than a training gap.

slides.title: Prove the customisation survives an upgrade
bullets: Property setters, custom fields and custom DocTypes live in the database, so they survive a migration
Hand-edited standard DocTypes and doctored core files do not, which is why the line matters
A migration can still rename a standard field underneath your setter, so verify after each upgrade
Test on staging first, with production data, then repeat the checks on production
Keep the register portable: a list a successor can read without opening the system
slides.notes: The upgrade test is what separates a configuration from a hack. Run it on staging, with production data, and compare the register against what the system actually does. Anything that no longer matches is either a broken setter or an undocumented change.

slides.title: Six columns that save a successor
bullets: Date, DocType, what changed, why, who asked and how to reverse it: six columns, nothing else
The reason matters more than the change, because it is the part nobody can reconstruct
Keep it outside the system as well, so it survives an outage and a handover
Review it with the client quarterly and delete what nobody uses, deliberately
A register that is a work of fiction is worse than none, so write the row when you make the change
slides.notes: The register is the cheapest insurance in a customisation-heavy project. Without it, the next consultant spends a week discovering twenty setters, and the client pays for that week. Write the row in the moment, not at the end of the project.

slides.title: The conversation that keeps the project supportable
bullets: When a requirement needs code, say so plainly and price it as development with its own testing and rollback
Offer the configuration alternative first: often field, workflow or report changes solve eighty per cent
Write the accepted gap into the scope document so it is a decision rather than an omission
A consultant who promises code and cannot deliver it damages the whole system's credibility
The client respects a clear boundary far more than a vague yes
slides.notes: The boundary conversation is a consultant skill, not an admin task. A vague yes buys a week of goodwill and costs a year of support. Offer the configuration path, name what code would cost, and record the decision — then the client owns it with you rather than blaming you for it.

lab.title: Lab · Customise a sales invoice and a site survey without code
steps: Draw up the configuration scope with the client and write the code boundary into it
Rename one label, make one field mandatory, and hide one field the business never uses
Create a custom field for the delivery site, place it correctly and show it in the list view
Verify the field as a normal sales user and confirm what it may and may not edit
Build a site survey DocType with its own naming series and one record
Add a findings child table with three columns and enter three findings on the survey
Reorganise the invoice form into two named sections and time a real user completing it
Run the upgrade checks, complete the change register and list every reversal step
lab.done: A documented set of browser-only customisations that a second role can use correctly, a custom DocType with a child table holding real data, and a six-column register with a reversal step for every change.

quiz.question: What actually separates configuration from development for a functional consultant?
options: The difficulty of the change
Whether the change needs a file, a deployment and a developer to reverse it
Whether the client has budget
Whether the field is custom or standard
quiz.why: Configuration is reversible in the browser and survives a migration; a file-based change needs a deployment and a rollback. That boundary is what decides whether you may promise it.

quiz.question: Why are property setters safer than editing the standard DocType directly?
options: They are faster to enter
The standard definition stays intact underneath and the override survives a migration
They require fewer permissions
They avoid the change register
quiz.why: A setter is an override stored on top of the standard definition, so an upgrade overwrites the standard, not your change, and the original behaviour remains recoverable.

quiz.question: What is the first decision that becomes hard to reverse on a custom DocType?
options: The permission list
The naming series, because every link depends on the names it produces
The field order in the form
Whether it is submittable
quiz.why: Once records exist under a series, renumbering them breaks every reference. Choose the series before the first save, and record why.

quiz.question: When does a custom field earn its place?
options: When the client asks for it
When someone filters, prints or reports on it
When the form has room for it
When it duplicates an existing field
quiz.why: A field nobody queries is an empty box waiting to be filled wrongly. Ask the reporting question before creating the column.

quiz.question: What belongs in a change register, beyond what changed?
options: The consultant's hours
Why it changed, who asked, and how to reverse it
The database table name
The stack trace of any error
quiz.why: The reason and the reversal are the parts a successor cannot reconstruct. Without them the register records facts but cannot restore behaviour.

memory.spine: Configuration is what you can reverse in the browser; everything else is development, and it is somebody else's promise.

device.label: Setters first, code last
expansion: Property setters change labels, mandatory and read-only without touching the standard
Custom fields need a reporting question before they need a type
A custom DocType needs its naming series decided before the first record
Child tables are for anything the client will count, sum or report per row
Every change gets a register row with its reason and its reversal

cards.q: How do you tell whether a request is configuration or development?
cards.a: If it can be made and reversed in the browser without a file or a deployment, it is configuration and it is yours. Otherwise it belongs to a developer.

cards.q: What does a property setter leave untouched underneath?
cards.a: The standard DocType definition. The override sits on top, so a migration replaces the standard and keeps the setter.

cards.q: Which custom DocType decision is hardest to undo and why?
cards.a: The naming series. Every record name is referenced by links, so renumbering later breaks them. Decide before the first save.

cards.q: When does a table field beat a long text field?
cards.a: When somebody will count, sum or report per line, such as findings by severity. Rows can be reported; prose cannot.

cards.q: What must the change register carry besides the change itself?
cards.a: The reason it was made, who asked for it, the date, and how to reverse it — plus a copy held outside the system.

trap.what: A promising sales demo ends with 'we can make it do anything', so three code changes are promised, none are priced, and go-live slips.
trap.why: Anything needing a file is development with its own testing and rollback. Offer the configuration path, price the code path, and record the gap as a decision the client owns.

narration: Most requirements a consultant hears can be met in the browser, and the value of knowing where that stops is what this chapter is for. Configuration is anything you can change and reverse in Customize Form: a property setter that renames a label, makes a field mandatory, hides it or makes it read-only, without touching the standard definition underneath. Custom fields come next, but only when somebody will filter, print or report on them, because a field nobody queries is an empty box. Then the DocType editor, where a functional consultant can build a new document with its own naming series and a child table for lines, provided the series is decided before the first record exists. Verify every change the same way: on the form, in the list, under a second role, and again after a migration on staging. Keep a six-column register, with the reason and the reversal, because that is the part the next consultant cannot reconstruct. And when a requirement genuinely needs code, say so plainly, price it, and write the gap down as a decision rather than letting a vague yes carry the project.
